# Garden Log October

## Harvest
I brought in the last of the green tomatoes on the 20th, a good 2 kg of them off the two outdoor plants that never ripened in the shortening days, and they are now laid out on a tray in the kitchen to ripen slowly or be turned into chutney if they refuse. The three squash came in the same week, fat and heavy, and they have gone onto the shelf in the shed to cure, where the skins will harden and they will keep through the winter. They were the best squash I have grown, ripened on the vine in the warm September and lifted before the first cold night touched them. The climbing beans were done by the second week and I cleared the whole row, cutting the stems at the base and putting the tops on the compost heap in layers with the soft prunings. The roots I left in the ground to break down over winter and feed the soil, which saves digging them out. The last few courgettes were picked small and eaten, though the plants were mildewed and tired by then. There is still kale standing, which will keep going until the hard frosts, and the leeks are ready whenever I want them. The apples came off the small tree by the shed, a poor crop this year, maybe a dozen in total, but sweet enough. The last of the chard was cut and the plants pulled, and the beetroot that had stood all summer came in too small to do much with but too good to waste. Taken as a whole it was a fair harvest rather than a great one, and the squash and the beans carried it.

## Sowings
The garlic went into the second plot on 8 October, from last year's own crop rather than shop bulbs, since I wanted to keep the strain that has done well here. I split the bulbs and chose the fattest cloves, planting them pointed end up and pressing them in so the tips sat just below the surface. The second plot drains better in winter, which is why the garlic lives there rather than in the first bed. I also sowed a row of broad beans for an early crop next spring, and they will sit quietly through the frosts and be away before anything else. On the far side I put in a small patch of winter salad under the cloche, rocket and a hardy lettuce, more in hope than expectation. I left the courgette bed bare for the winter rather than sowing a green manure, since I wanted to spread compost there first and let it settle. The winter salad is a gamble in a cold plot, but the cloche gives it a chance and the rocket usually comes through. I have left the strawberry bed alone and will tidy it in the spring, when the runners can be potted up. Nothing else goes in now, since the ground is cooling and seed would only rot rather than grow.

## Notes
I spread a good 5 cm of straw mulch over the garlic and the beans, partly to hold the moisture and partly to keep the worst of the frost off the soil. The beds are tucked up for winter now, the compost heap is full and the tools have been cleaned and hung in the shed. The one job left is to empty the tomato pots and wash them before they go into storage. I am leaving the greenhouse glass alone until the frosts come, then I will scrub it so the light gets in for the spring sowings. Nothing tender left outside now, so the garden can look after itself until the turn of the year. I have made a note in the shed book of what went where, so next spring I can rotate the beds properly rather than guessing. The seed tins have been sorted and the packets past their date thrown out, which is a job I put off every year. It is a quiet month, and that is part of the pleasure of it.
